turn_text: David, walk us through this a little bit as to why this ban on the so-called revolving door is so important. What happens when lawmakers are able to immediately transition from being a legislator to being a lobbyist?

Well, for one thing, they don't just walk out and have a job ready the next day without having had any prior conversations. They typically we find have had some sort of conversation informally so, and legally we would hope beforehand. It's not as if they necessarily trade votes for in order to get jobs, but they might not be quite as vigilant in terms of their oversight responsibilities or their treatment of perspective. employers while serving. It just has a corrosive, the idea that lawmakers are mainly thinking about their next job a lot of times while they're in the legislature is corrosive to a representative government. And as we talk to people in the legislature, we do find they very much have their minds on what comes next. And one issue that has some legitimacy that's been raised is that there's an equity issue here. That people who come from minority communities in particular, for them, this job is an important one and their next one is important to them. And they don't have as many options as other people might have. And so that issue has been raised and it's one that needs to be taken seriously because there is some basis to it. But overall, we've seen a very kind of a negative outcome when people just walk out of the legislature and begin lobbying for a client that whose business they might have been overseeing just days earlier while a member of the body.
And care to venture any guesses as to the likelihood that lawmakers will pass something that will dramatically limit their employment opportunities once they leave office?

Sadly, when you look at the history of reform in the state legislature, we've seen bouts of ethics reform previously.
